screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: In this section you'll see four concrete learning goals that prepare you to design and secure private connectivity from your applications. First, you will understand the purpose and benefits of VPC Endpoints, including why they keep traffic on the AWS network and how that supports compliance and performance. Second, you will distinguish Interface Endpoints, which create ENIs and support many services, from Gateway Endpoints, which act as route targets specifically for S3 and DynamoDB. Third, you will learn how to configure endpoints so applications in private subnets can interact with services without using a NAT Gateway or the public internet. Practice will include route table associations and DNS behavior. Fourth, you will implement IAM and endpoint policies to restrict who can use an endpoint and enforce network-origin conditions. Each objective includes a short rationale: these skills remove a frequent barrier when moving sensitive workloads into private subnets and help you avoid common security mistakes. By the end, you'll be able to choose the correct endpoint type, provision it, and validate both network and identity controls in a working environment.

screens.title: Learning Objectives — Details & Rationale
screens.narratorSegment: Let's expand each learning objective with its practical rationale. You will first grasp the endpoint concept as a virtual device that keeps service traffic inside AWS. That improves latency and security because packets don't traverse the public internet. Next, distinguishing Gateway and Interface endpoints matters operationally: Gateway endpoints change route tables and cost nothing, whereas Interface endpoints create ENIs and incur hourly and data processing charges. Knowing this avoids surprise bills and architecture mistakes. Then you'll practice configuration steps: create the endpoint, associate the right route tables or subnets, enable private DNS, and check that SDK DNS resolves to private IPs. These are precise steps that make private access work without code changes. Finally, you'll apply IAM and endpoint policies so that identity controls complement network controls; for example, restrict S3 access to requests originating from your VPC. That layered approach prevents unauthorized access even if network controls are misapplied. Completing these objectives helps you design secure, compliant systems that keep sensitive traffic off the public internet.

screens.title: NAT Gateway vs VPC Endpoints
screens.narratorSegment: A NAT Gateway lets instances in private subnets initiate outbound connections to the internet, but it does so by routing traffic out through a public IP. That means your request leaves the AWS network and can traverse the public internet before reaching the AWS service, which can violate some security or compliance rules and can add latency. VPC Endpoints provide a private alternative: Gateway Endpoints route service traffic at the route table level to a virtual target, while Interface Endpoints create ENIs that present private IPs for service access. A concrete example: a logging service running on a private EC2 that must upload logs to S3. If you use a NAT Gateway, those uploads will travel to S3's public endpoints; if the security team requires private-only traffic, a Gateway Endpoint for S3 ensures traffic remains on the Amazon backbone. A common misconception is assuming NAT is always acceptable for outbound service calls; in regulated environments, that assumption can fail audits. The takeaway is simple: use NAT for general internet access and diagnostics, but prefer endpoints when you need guaranteed private service connectivity and compliance-friendly architecture. How would you decide which services need endpoints in your application architecture?

keyIdea.title: Decision rule
keyIdea.text: Use NAT for generic internet access; use VPC Endpoints to keep service traffic inside AWS and meet security or compliance needs.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.2 › NAT Gateway vs VPC Endpoints
Comparison overview
NAT Gateway
  • Routes private traffic to the internet using public IPs.
  • Useful for package downloads, updates, and outbound calls to arbitrary endpoints.
  • Does not guarantee traffic stays on the AWS network.
VPC Endpoints
  • Keep traffic within AWS for supported services.
  • Gateway for S3/DynamoDB; Interface for many other services.
  • Improve security and can reduce external exposure and latency.
Key Takeaway

Choose endpoints when you must ensure service calls never traverse the public internet; use NAT for general outbound connectivity.

Concrete example

A private EC2 needs to upload files to an S3 bucket under a compliance policy that forbids internet egress. Creating a Gateway Endpoint for S3 and associating it with the private subnet's route table keeps uploads on the Amazon backbone and satisfies that requirement.

Common misconception

Believing NAT alone is secure enough for all service calls. NAT does not keep traffic confined to AWS, so it may fail compliance checks.

Pro tip: Inventory which services your apps call and map each to gateway, interface, or public endpoints to plan costs and security.

screens.title: What is a VPC Endpoint?
screens.narratorSegment: A VPC Endpoint is a virtual device that enables private connectivity between resources in your VPC and supported AWS services or endpoint services powered by PrivateLink. Unlike an Internet Gateway or NAT Gateway, an endpoint provides a controlled, private path so instances use private IP addresses when calling a service. For Gateway Endpoints, AWS updates route tables to direct service-destined traffic to the endpoint target. For Interface Endpoints, AWS creates Elastic Network Interfaces with private IPs inside your chosen subnets and optionally associates Security Groups with those ENIs to control access. From a developer's perspective this is mostly transparent: the AWS SDK resolves the service DNS to the endpoint's private IPs when private DNS is enabled. A practical example: you have a Lambda or EC2 role that calls SQS; with an Interface Endpoint the SDK call resolves privately and the traffic never leaves the AWS network. A common misconception is thinking endpoints replace IAM; they do not. Endpoints change the network path but you still need identity policies to control which principals can call the service. Reflect on this definition and ask: does my service need a private path, or are public endpoints acceptable for my data sensitivity level?

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.2 › What is a VPC Endpoint?
Precise definition

A virtual device enabling private connections between a VPC and supported AWS services or PrivateLink-powered services. It prevents traffic from going out to the public internet for supported services.

Why it changes behavior
  • Gateway Endpoints modify route tables for S3/DynamoDB.
  • Interface Endpoints create ENIs with private IP addresses for wider service support.
  • SDK and DNS resolution return private IPs when private DNS is enabled.
Concrete example

An application writes telemetry to an S3 bucket. With a Gateway Endpoint for S3, the route table sends S3 traffic to the endpoint so the data stays inside AWS instead of going via a NAT Gateway and the public internet.

Misconception check

Endpoints do not replace IAM. They provide private transport; you still need identity policies to control who can access a service.

Pro tip: Plan endpoints by service and compliance need to avoid unexpected costs and access gaps.

screens.title: Gateway Endpoints — S3 and DynamoDB
screens.narratorSegment: Gateway Endpoints are a special type of VPC Endpoint built for S3 and DynamoDB. When you create a Gateway Endpoint you select the VPC and one or more route tables; AWS then inserts a route that points service traffic to the endpoint. This approach is simple and cost-free: there are no network interfaces created in your subnets and no hourly endpoint charge. A practical use case is a private EC2 that uploads application logs to S3. By associating the private subnet's route table with the S3 Gateway Endpoint, calls to S3 use the private route. From a developer's view, no code changes are required; SDK calls resolve and follow the private route when the route table has the endpoint. A common mistake is forgetting to associate the correct route table: if your private subnet's route table is not configured, traffic will still follow the default route and may use a NAT Gateway. Another consideration: Gateway Endpoint policies let you restrict which principals can access the service via that endpoint. The core idea is that Gateway Endpoints are cost-effective and reliable for S3 and DynamoDB access within a VPC.

keyIdea.title: Gateway summary
keyIdea.text: Gateway Endpoints route traffic at the route table level for S3 and DynamoDB, require no ENIs, and are free to use.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.2 › Gateway Endpoints — S3 and DynamoDB
Mechanics
  • Create endpoint and select route tables for association.
  • A route is added pointing traffic for S3 or DynamoDB to the endpoint target.
  • No ENIs are created; there is no hourly endpoint charge.
Verification

Check the private subnet's route table for a new entry pointing to the Gateway Endpoint identifier (pl-xxxxxx).

Example scenario

A batch job on private instances archives results to S3. You create a Gateway Endpoint for S3 and attach the private subnet route table so uploads never leave AWS's internal network.

Common mistake

Not associating the correct route table. Verify every private subnet that needs S3 access points to the endpoint route, otherwise traffic may still exit via NAT.

Key Takeaway: Gateway Endpoints are simple and cost-free for S3/DynamoDB — ensure route tables are associated.

screens.title: Interface Endpoints and PrivateLink
screens.narratorSegment: Interface Endpoints, powered by AWS PrivateLink, let your VPC privately connect to many AWS services and endpoint services offered by other accounts. When you create an Interface Endpoint you choose one or more subnets; AWS then creates Elastic Network Interfaces (ENIs) in those subnets. Each ENI receives a private IP address and can have Security Groups attached. Traffic to the service flows through those ENIs, meaning you can apply Security Group rules to control which producers may reach the service. Interface Endpoints are charged per hour and per GB of data processed, so they come with a cost trade-off compared to Gateway Endpoints. An example: if your application publishes to SQS from a private subnet, create an Interface Endpoint for SQS and attach a Security Group that allows inbound HTTPS from the application's Security Group. A frequent misconfiguration is forgetting to allow inbound HTTPS from the app's SG to the endpoint's SG and the reverse outbound rule — without both, the connection will be blocked even though the endpoint exists. The practical takeaway is that Interface Endpoints offer broader service support but require explicit Security Group planning and cost consideration.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.2 › Interface Endpoints and PrivateLink
How they work
  • Creates ENIs with private IPs in specified subnets.
  • Attach Security Groups to those ENIs to control access.
  • Supports a wide range of AWS services through PrivateLink.
Operational note

Plan subnet selection so ENIs are reachable from your application subnets and consider cross-AZ redundancy by selecting subnets in multiple AZs.

Concrete example

A backend in a private subnet publishes to SQS. Create an Interface Endpoint for SQS in the same AZ subnets, attach a Security Group that allows inbound HTTPS from the backend's Security Group, and enable private DNS to let SDK calls resolve to the ENI IPs.

Common mistake

Omitting Security Group rules or selecting subnets that are isolated from your application traffic path results in blocked connections even when the endpoint exists.

Pro tip: Mirror endpoint Security Group rules so both the app SG and endpoint SG allow the expected 443 traffic between them.

screens.title: DNS resolution and SDK behavior
screens.narratorSegment: When you enable private DNS for a VPC Endpoint, the DNS names your SDKs normally use resolve to the endpoint's private IP addresses inside the VPC. This is important because it means you typically do not need to change application code: the SDK will call the same logical endpoint name, but DNS inside the VPC now points to a private address. For example, if you enable private DNS on an Interface Endpoint for SQS, calls to the standard SQS hostname will resolve privately. Verification steps include using a private EC2 to run a DNS lookup for the service hostname and confirming it returns an IP within your VPC. A common pitfall is not enabling private DNS or testing resolution from outside the VPC; DNS changes only affect the VPC's resolver. Also, the SDK will honor the resolved address, so ensure Security Groups and IAM are configured correctly. As a quick diagnostic workflow: check DNS resolution, confirm Security Group pairings between the application SG and the endpoint SG, and validate IAM permissions. One final question: when you run a DNS lookup from your private instance, what address range would confirm private resolution versus a public endpoint?

keyIdea.text: Private DNS causes standard service hostnames to resolve to endpoint private IPs inside the VPC, making endpoint usage transparent to application code.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.2 › DNS resolution and SDK behavior
Explanation

Private DNS rewrites service hostnames inside your VPC so the name resolves to the endpoint's private IPs. The SDK continues to call the same hostname, but the network path is private.

Verification checklist
  • Run a DNS lookup from a private instance for the service hostname.
  • Confirm the returned IP is from your VPC or endpoint ENI range.
  • Ensure Security Group rules permit traffic to the ENI IP on port 443.
Code / command example
# From a private EC2 instance
# Use the system resolver to check DNS
nslookup sqs.us-east-1.amazonaws.com

# Or use dig if available
dig +short sqs.us-east-1.amazonaws.com

# Expected: private IP(s) that match your ENI or VPC CIDR ranges
Misconception

Private DNS affects only the VPC resolver. External machines or developer workstations will still resolve the public endpoint unless they use the VPC resolver or VPN into the VPC.

screens.title: Creating an Interface Endpoint via the CLI
screens.narratorSegment: In production you will often script endpoint creation. The AWS CLI command to create an Interface Endpoint requires a VPC ID, the endpoint type set to Interface, the service name, subnet IDs for ENI placement, and Security Group IDs. Enabling private DNS ensures standard hostnames resolve privately. When using the CLI, first identify your VPC and subnets; then run the create-vpc-endpoint command. A concrete example is creating an Interface Endpoint for SQS. Note that the service name is region-specific and follows the com. amazonaws. REGION. SERVICE pattern. A critical detail is the Security Group you attach to the endpoint ENIs: it must allow inbound HTTPS from your application. Also, remember to consider cross-AZ subnet selection for resilience. Finally, after creation, verify ENIs exist in the chosen subnets and run DNS checks. This workflow automates endpoint provisioning and makes it repeatable across environments. Creating an Interface Endpoint via the CLI means use the aws cli to create interface endpoints by specifying vpc, subnets, security groups, and enabling private dns to make endpoints immediately usable by sdks.. In practical terms, a practical cli example and what each flag does. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.2 › Creating an Interface Endpoint via the CLI
CLI example
# Example: Create an Interface Endpoint for SQS
aws ec2 create-vpc-endpoint \
    --vpc-id vpc-0abcdef1234567890 \
    --vpc-endpoint-type Interface \
    --service-name com.amazonaws.us-east-1.sqs \
    --subnet-ids subnet-0123456789abcdef0 subnet-0fedcba9876543210 \
    --security-group-ids sg-0abcdef1234567890 \
    --private-dns-enabled
vpc-id, subnet-ids
Choose the VPC and subnets where ENIs will be created; pick subnets across AZs for resilience.
security-group-ids
Attach SGs that allow inbound HTTPS from your application SGs.
Pro tip: After creation, inspect ENIs and test DNS resolution from a private instance before relying on the endpoint in production.

screens.title: Security Groups and ENI pairings
screens.narratorSegment: A very common cause of failed endpoint connectivity is Security Group misconfiguration. Interface Endpoints create ENIs that have Security Groups; your application has its own Security Group. For traffic to flow, the endpoint ENI's Security Group must allow inbound HTTPS (TCP 443) from the application's Security Group. Conversely, the application's Security Group must allow outbound HTTPS to the endpoint's Security Group. Many teams mistakenly only configure one side or assume default rules allow the traffic. A concrete example: your backend's SG permits outbound 0.0.0.0/0 on port 443, but the endpoint's SG is locked to a specific CIDR and does not include the backend SG; this will block the traffic. To avoid mistakes, follow a pairing pattern: create a dedicated endpoint SG that allows HTTPS inbound from app SGs, tag both SGs, and document the pairing. Steps to debug include verifying ENI presence, checking SG inbound/outbound rules, and testing connectivity with curl or openssl s_client to the resolved endpoint IP. The takeaway: manage both sides of the SG relationship explicitly to ensure reliable endpoint connectivity. Security Groups and ENI pairings means ensure security group rules are configured on both the application and endpoint eni sides — missing rules on either side block traffic.. In practical terms, common misconfigurations and how to avoid them. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

A concrete example: your backend's SG permits outbound 0.0.0.0/0 on port 443, but the endpoint's SG is locked to a specific CIDR and does not include the backend SG; this will block the traffic. To avoid mistakes, follow a pairing pattern: create a dedicated endpoint SG that allows HTTPS inbound from app SGs, tag both SGs, and document the pairing. Steps to debug include verifying ENI presence, checking SG inbound/outbound rules, and testing connectivity with curl or openssl s_client to the resolved endpoint IP. The takeaway: manage both sides of the SG relationship explicitly to ensure reliable endpoint connectivity. Security Groups and ENI pairings means ensure security group rules are configured on both the application and endpoint eni sides — missing rules on either side block traffic.. Module 5 › Chapter 5.2 › Security Groups and ENI pairings
Pairing pattern
  1. Create an endpoint Security Group that allows inbound TCP 443 from your application SG.
  2. Ensure application SG allows outbound TCP 443 to the endpoint SG or CIDR.
  3. Attach the endpoint SG when creating the Interface Endpoint so ENIs inherit it.
Debug checklist
  • Confirm ENIs exist in the expected subnets.
  • Check inbound rules on the endpoint SG and outbound rules on the app SG.
  • Test connectivity to the private IP on port 443 using curl or openssl.
Quick example

Endpoint SG inbound: allow TCP 443 from sg-app (source = security-group-id). App SG outbound: allow TCP 443 to sg-endpoint (destination = security-group-id).

Common mistake: relying on default outbound rules only. Explicit SG pairing prevents intermittent failures and unclear logs.

screens.title: Endpoint Policies and IAM Controls
screens.narratorSegment: While VPC Endpoints provide a private transport, they do not replace IAM-based access controls. Endpoint policies are resource policies attached to an endpoint that can restrict which principals or actions are allowed through that endpoint. For Gateway Endpoints you can attach an endpoint policy to limit who can use the endpoint to access S3 or DynamoDB. For Interface Endpoints, access control is typically handled via IAM permissions on the calling principal plus Security Group rules on the ENIs. A concrete policy example is adding a condition on a bucket policy to permit GetObject only when the request originates from a specific VPC ID. This enforces network-origin constraints at the resource level. A common misconception is thinking network-only controls fully protect resources; without IAM or endpoint policies, an entity with valid credentials from an authorized VPC could still access a resource. Best practice is layered security: apply strict IAM least-privilege, add endpoint policies where appropriate, and ensure Security Groups block unwanted traffic. Consider writing a bucket policy that checks aws:SourceVpc or using endpoint policies to explicitly deny undesired principals. Endpoint Policies and IAM Controls means use endpoint policies, iam permissions, and security groups together to control both who can access a service and from where.. In practical terms, combining network and identity-level restrictions. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.2 › Endpoint Policies and IAM Controls
How endpoint policies work

Endpoint policies are resource policies attached to a VPC Endpoint that can allow or deny actions through that endpoint, restricting which principals may use it.

Example condition
{
  "Version": "2012-10-17",
  "Statement": [
    {
      "Effect": "Allow",
      "Principal": "*",
      "Action": "s3:GetObject",
      "Resource": "arn:aws:s3:::my-private-bucket/*",
      "Condition": {
        "StringEquals": { "aws:SourceVpc": "vpc-0abcdef1234567890" }
      }
    }
  ]
}
Practical guidance
  • Use endpoint policies to restrict use of a Gateway Endpoint to specific principals.
  • For Interface Endpoints, rely on IAM on the caller plus endpoint SGs to control network access.
  • Always follow least privilege and test policy+network interactions together.
Key Takeaway: Identity controls complement network controls — use both to defend resources.

screens.title: Activity: Secure S3 Access from a Private EC2
screens.narratorSegment: This guided activity walks you through creating a Gateway Endpoint so a private EC2 instance can upload to S3 without using a NAT Gateway. Start by confirming you have a VPC with a private subnet and an EC2 instance in that subnet. Ensure the EC2 role has s3:PutObject and s3:GetObject permissions for your bucket. Create an S3 bucket and then in the VPC console create a Gateway Endpoint for S3. When asked, select your VPC and choose the private subnet's route table(s) for association; AWS will add a route entry that points S3 traffic to the endpoint. After creation, SSH into the private instance via a bastion host and run an upload test: create a short file, run aws s3 cp to upload it, then list the bucket to verify. To confirm the upload used the endpoint rather than NAT, inspect the route table for the new S3 route and verify the instance's traffic to S3 resolves to a private path using VPC DNS. A common check is looking for the pl- identifier in the route table. Reflect: how does this flow meet your compliance requirement to avoid internet egress?

screens.title: Troubleshooting and Best Practices
screens.narratorSegment: When endpoints don't work as expected, a structured troubleshooting approach saves time. First, confirm the endpoint exists and is associated with the right route table or subnets. For Gateway Endpoints check the route table entry; for Interface Endpoints check ENIs in the chosen subnets. Second, validate DNS resolution from a private instance to ensure private DNS is enabled and returning endpoint IPs. Third, inspect Security Groups on both the endpoint and the application: make sure inbound and outbound HTTPS rules align and reference the correct security-group IDs. Fourth, verify IAM and endpoint policies: permissions errors can masquerade as network failures. As an example, an app calling Kinesis via an Interface Endpoint may see connection timeouts if the endpoint's SG blocks inbound 443 traffic; if IAM is missing the PutRecord permission, you may get authorization errors instead. Best practices include selecting subnets across AZs for endpoint ENIs, documenting SG pairings, and applying least-privilege IAM combined with endpoint policies. Finally, add logging and a simple connectivity test to your deployment pipeline to surface endpoint regressions early. Which of these checks would you automate in your deployment pipeline?

screens.title: Key Concepts
screens.narratorSegment: Let's summarize the most important concepts. fullNarratorScript:
In this chapter we will explore how applications running inside private subnets can reach AWS services without crossing the public internet. You will learn what VPC Endpoints are, the two endpoint types — Gateway and Interface — and when to use each. We'll examine how DNS resolution and SDK behavior route calls to endpoints, review the security controls you must configure, and walk through a hands-on S3 activity. This matters because many compliance and security requirements forbid routing sensitive data over the public internet, and using the wrong mechanism can break an otherwise working application. For example, a private EC2 instance can upload logs to S3 through a Gateway Endpoint so the data never leaves the AWS network. We'll also highlight common misconfigurations developers make, like forgetting Security Group rules on Interface Endpoint ENIs or omitting endpoint IAM policies. By the end of the lesson you'll know which endpoint type is required for each service, how to provision an endpoint via CLI or console, and how to combine network-level and identity-level controls to build a secure, private application architecture. Consider how your current applications rely on public endpoints and which ones should be migrated to private endpoints.

In this section you'll see four concrete learning goals that prepare you to design and secure private connectivity from your applications. First, you will understand the purpose and benefits of VPC Endpoints, including why they keep traffic on the AWS network and how that supports compliance and performance. Second, you will distinguish Interface Endpoints, which create ENIs and support many services, from Gateway Endpoints, which act as route targets specifically for S3 and DynamoDB. Third, you will learn how to configure endpoints so applications in private subnets can interact with services without using a NAT Gateway or the public internet. Practice will include route table associations and DNS behavior. Fourth, you will implement IAM and endpoint policies to restrict who can use an endpoint and enforce network-origin conditions. Each objective includes a short rationale: these skills remove a frequent barrier when moving sensitive workloads into private subnets and help you avoid common security mistakes. By the end, you'll be able to choose the correct endpoint type, provision it, and validate both network and identity controls in a working environment.

Let's expand each learning objective with its practical rationale. You will first grasp the endpoint concept as a virtual device that keeps service traffic inside AWS. That improves latency and security because packets don't traverse the public internet. Next, distinguishing Gateway and Interface endpoints matters operationally: Gateway endpoints change route tables and cost nothing, whereas Interface endpoints create ENIs and incur hourly and data processing charges. Knowing this avoids surprise bills and architecture mistakes. Then you'll practice configuration steps: create the endpoint, associate the right route tables or subnets, enable private DNS, and check that SDK DNS resolves to private IPs. These are precise steps that make private access work without code changes. Finally, you'll apply IAM and endpoint policies so that identity controls complement network controls; for example, restrict S3 access to requests originating from your VPC. That layered approach prevents unauthorized access even if network controls are misapplied. Completing these objectives helps you design secure, compliant systems that keep sensitive traffic off the public internet.

A NAT Gateway lets instances in private subnets initiate outbound connections to the internet, but it does so by routing traffic out through a public IP. That means your request leaves the AWS network and can traverse the public internet before reaching the AWS service, which can violate some security or compliance rules and can add latency. VPC Endpoints provide a private alternative: Gateway Endpoints route service traffic at the route table level to a virtual target, while Interface Endpoints create ENIs that present private IPs for service access. A concrete example: a logging service running on a private EC2 that must upload logs to S3. If you use a NAT Gateway, those uploads will travel to S3's public endpoints; if the security team requires private-only traffic, a Gateway Endpoint for S3 ensures traffic remains on the Amazon backbone. A common misconception is assuming NAT is always acceptable for outbound service calls; in regulated environments, that assumption can fail audits. The takeaway is simple: use NAT for general internet access and diagnostics, but prefer endpoints when you need guaranteed private service connectivity and compliance-friendly architecture. How would you decide which services need endpoints in your application architecture?

A VPC Endpoint is a virtual device that enables private connectivity between resources in your VPC and supported AWS services or endpoint services powered by PrivateLink. Unlike an Internet Gateway or NAT Gateway, an endpoint provides a controlled, private path so instances use private IP addresses when calling a service. For Gateway Endpoints, AWS updates route tables to direct service-destined traffic to the endpoint target. For Interface Endpoints, AWS creates Elastic Network Interfaces with private IPs inside your chosen subnets and optionally associates Security Groups with those ENIs to control access. From a developer's perspective this is mostly transparent: the AWS SDK resolves the service DNS to the endpoint's private IPs when private DNS is enabled. A practical example: you have a Lambda or EC2 role that calls SQS; with an Interface Endpoint the SDK call resolves privately and the traffic never leaves the AWS network. A common misconception is thinking endpoints replace IAM; they do not. Endpoints change the network path but you still need identity policies to control which principals can call the service. Reflect on this definition and ask: does my service need a private path, or are public endpoints acceptable for my data sensitivity level?

Gateway Endpoints are a special type of VPC Endpoint built for S3 and DynamoDB. When you create a Gateway Endpoint you select the VPC and one or more route tables; AWS then inserts a route that points service traffic to the endpoint. This approach is simple and cost-free: there are no network interfaces created in your subnets and no hourly endpoint charge. A practical use case is a private EC2 that uploads application logs to S3. By associating the private subnet's route table with the S3 Gateway Endpoint, calls to S3 use the private route. From a developer's view, no code changes are required; SDK calls resolve and follow the private route when the route table has the endpoint. A common mistake is forgetting to associate the correct route table: if your private subnet's route table is not configured, traffic will still follow the default route and may use a NAT Gateway. Another consideration: Gateway Endpoint policies let you restrict which principals can access the service via that endpoint. The core idea is that Gateway Endpoints are cost-effective and reliable for S3 and DynamoDB access within a VPC.

Interface Endpoints, powered by AWS PrivateLink, let your VPC privately connect to many AWS services and endpoint services offered by other accounts. When you create an Interface Endpoint you choose one or more subnets; AWS then creates Elastic Network Interfaces (ENIs) in those subnets. Each ENI receives a private IP address and can have Security Groups attached. A common pitfall is not enabling private DNS or testing resolution from outside the VPC; DNS changes only affect the VPC's resolver. Also, the SDK will honor the resolved address, so ensure Security Groups and IAM are configured correctly. First, a VPC Endpoint is a virtual device that provides private connectivity between your VPC and supported AWS services so traffic does not traverse the public internet. Second, Gateway Endpoints are used specifically for S3 and DynamoDB, operate by adding route table entries, and are free to use. Third, Interface Endpoints are powered by PrivateLink, create ENIs with private IPs in specified subnets, support many AWS services, and require Security Group planning and incur charges. Keep these three facts in mind when designing private connectivity: the endpoint type determines operational steps, costs, and the security pattern you must follow. As you design, ask which services require private transport, which cost model fits your budget, and whether your Security Groups and IAM policies are prepared to enforce access. These three concepts form the foundation for secure, private service access in your VPC.

A few additional concepts complete the picture. First, Private DNS makes endpoint usage transparent by resolving standard service hostnames to private IP addresses inside the VPC, so most SDK calls require no code changes. Second, Security Group pairing between application SGs and endpoint ENI SGs is essential for Interface Endpoints — missing inbound or outbound rules will block traffic even when the endpoint exists. Third, endpoint policies and IAM conditions such as aws:SourceVpc let you enforce who and where requests may originate, providing layered protection. Together, these ideas form a reliable approach: enable private DNS for transparency, plan and test Security Group rules for connectivity, and apply IAM and endpoint policies for identity-level restrictions. Before closing, consider which of these controls you will add to your deployment checklist to prevent configuration drift and audit failures.
